section.title: Completeness and the idea of no gaps
section.p: The last section used the real line as if every point on it had a number. That is a stronger promise than it may first appear.
Fractions are already very rich. Between any two fractions there is another fraction. For example, between 1.41 and 1.42 lies
Still, fractions alone leave gaps. Geometry finds one of those gaps in a unit square.

note.title: First-reading note
note.p: This section explains why the real numbers, not only rational numbers, are the right setting for calculus. You may read the proof details lightly on a first pass. The main idea is simple: calculus needs an unbroken number line because limits can point to numbers that no finite decimal or fraction exactly equals.

remark.title: Moral
remark.p: Fractions can approximate the diagonal of a unit square as closely as we want, but no fraction equals it.

subsection.p: This is the first warning that many numbers is not the same as no gaps.

subsection.p: The decimal approximations to \sqrt{2} give a sequence of smaller and smaller intervals:

figure.caption: Nested intervals trap one number. For the real line, that trapped point exists. For the rational numbers alone, this example traps a missing point.

subsection.p: This picture leads to a principle.

statement.p: is a nested sequence of closed intervals I_n=[a_n,b_n], and the lengths b_n-a_n become arbitrarily small. Then there is exactly one real number that lies in every interval I_n.

subsection.p: For the intervals above, that one real number is \sqrt{2}.

paragraphs.title: Idea of the proof
paragraphs.p: The left endpoints a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots move to the right or stay fixed. The right endpoints b_1, b_2, b_3, \dots move to the left or stay fixed. Since every left endpoint is still to the left of every right endpoint, the left endpoints are bounded above.

The real numbers have a least upper bound for the left endpoints. Call it L. Then L lies in every closed interval. If two different numbers x\lt y lay in every interval, then every interval would have length at least y-x. But the interval lengths become arbitrarily small. Therefore there can be only one such number.
This proof depends on the fact that the left endpoints have a least upper bound. That fact is one form of completeness (absence of holes) of real numbers.

paragraphs.title: What goes wrong with rational numbers
paragraphs.p: Take the same nested intervals, but allow only rational numbers. Each interval contains many rational numbers. Their lengths shrink toward 0. But the only real number common to all of them is \sqrt{2}, and \sqrt{2} is not rational.
So inside the rational numbers alone, these nested rational intervals have no rational point in common. That is a gap.

subsection.title: Least upper bound property
subsection.p: Completeness can be stated in several equivalent ways. The most useful form for proofs is the least upper bound property. First we need two definitions.

statement.p: Let S be a set of real numbers. A number M is an upper bound for S if x\le M for every x\in S.
A number L is the least upper bound of S if L is an upper bound for S, and no smaller number is an upper bound for S.
The least upper bound is also called the supremum of S, written \sup S.
Let S=(0,1). Then 1 is an upper bound for S, because every number in (0,1) is less than 1.
So is 2. So is 100. But 1 is the least upper bound: \sup(0,1)=1.
Notice that 1 is not in the set (0,1). A set does not need to contain its least upper bound.
This time the set does contain its least upper bound. In this case, 1 is also the maximum of the set.

remark.title: Maximum versus least upper bound
remark.p: A maximum must belong to the set.
A least upper bound may or may not belong to the set.

principle.title: Completeness Property of the Real Numbers

statement.p: Every nonempty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound.

subsection.p: This property is what fills the gaps. It is not true for the rational numbers.

paragraphs.title: The rational counterexample
paragraphs.p: Let
This is a nonempty set of rational numbers. For example, 1\in A_{\mathbb{Q}}. It is bounded above. For example, 2 is an upper bound.
But A_{\mathbb{Q}}, viewed only inside the rational numbers, has no least upper bound. The boundary should be \sqrt{2}, but \sqrt{2}\notin\mathbb{Q}.
The rational line has a hole exactly where the least upper bound should be.

subsection.title: Completeness creates \sqrt{2}
subsection.p: The completeness property does more than describe \sqrt{2}. It guarantees that such a number exists.

paragraphs.title: Optional proof
paragraphs.p: Let
The set A is nonempty because 1\in A. It is bounded above because no number x\ge 2 can satisfy x^2\lt 2.
By completeness, A has a least upper bound. Call it \alpha:
We will show that \alpha^2=2. There are three possibilities: \alpha^2\lt 2, \alpha^2=2, or \alpha^2\gt 2. We rule out the first and third.

Since 0\lt \eta\lt 1, we have \eta^2\lt \eta, so
Thus \alpha+\eta\in A. But \alpha+\eta\gt \alpha, contradicting that \alpha is an upper bound for A. Therefore \alpha^2\lt 2 is impossible.
Now suppose that \alpha^2\gt 2. Choose a positive number \eta so small that
Then \alpha-\eta\gt 0, and
If x\ge \alpha-\eta, then x^2\ge(\alpha-\eta)^2\gt 2, so x\notin A. Therefore every x\in A satisfies x\lt \alpha-\eta.
This means that \alpha-\eta is an upper bound for A, smaller than \alpha. That contradicts the fact that \alpha is the least upper bound. Therefore \alpha^2\gt 2 is impossible.
The only remaining possibility is \alpha^2=2. So the real number \alpha is the number whose square is 2. We call it \sqrt{2}.

remark.title: What the proof showed
remark.p: The existence of \sqrt{2} is not a decimal accident. It follows from the no-gaps property of the real numbers.

subsection.title: Why calculus needs the real numbers
subsection.p: Calculus builds exact numbers from limiting processes.

A tangent slope is approached by slopes of secant lines. An area is approached by sums of thin rectangles. A root can be trapped by bisection inside smaller and smaller intervals. An infinite decimal is approached by its finite decimal truncations.
Each step in such a process may use rational numbers. But the number approached may be irrational.
The rational numbers are excellent for computation. They are not complete enough for calculus.

example.title: Bisection finds a missing rational point

statement.p: Start with the interval [1,2]. Since 1^2\lt 2\lt 2^2, the solution, if it exists, should lie between 1 and 2.
Bisect the interval. Since 1.5^2=2.25\gt 2, the solution lies in [1,1.5].
Bisect again. Since 1.25^2=1.5625\lt 2, the solution lies in [1.25,1.5].
Continuing forever gives nested intervals whose lengths shrink to 0. The real number trapped by this process is \sqrt{2}. If we allowed only rational numbers, the process would point to a hole.

paragraphs.title: The calculus lesson
paragraphs.p: A limiting process is a promise that approximations have a destination. Completeness says that, for the real line, the destination exists.
We will not mention completeness every time we take a limit. But it is quietly underneath the whole subject. It is what lets the language of as close as we want point to an actual number.

The real line gives us numbers and distances. The next step is to let one number determine another. A temperature depends on time. A position depends on time. An error depends on a step size h. Those dependencies are called functions.
